channel.title: AI Stupa Translation Project
channel.description: New English translations of texts from the Tibetan Buddhist canon, made by the AI Stupa (provisional, public domain).

item.title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra called The Samādhi in Which the Buddhas of the Present Stand Directly Before One (Toh 133)
item.description: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra called The Samādhi in Which the Buddhas of the Present Stand Directly Before One, known in Sanskrit as the Pratyutpannabuddhasaṃmukhāvasthitasamādhi Sūtra and in Tibetan as Phakpa Datar Gyi Sangye Ngönsum Du Zhukpé Tingngé Dzin, is a Mahāyāna discourse on a meditative absorption through which a practitioner comes to behold the buddhas of the present age as if they…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called Six Doors (Toh 141)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called Six Doors, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Ṣaḍmukha Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Phakpa Go Drukpa Zhejawé Zung, is a short dhāraṇī text, a formula meant to be memorized and recited for spiritual benefit. It opens with homage to the youthful Mañjuśrī and is set in a jeweled assembly courtyard suspended in the sky above the Pure Abodes, where the Buddha addresses a vast…

item.title: Dhāraṇī for Not Forgetting (The Dhāraṇī of Avalokiteśvara for Retention) (Toh 1044)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Learning a Thousand Ślokas is a brief incantation text that pairs a short mantra with a simple ritual recipe for strengthening memory and learning. After paying homage to the Three Jewels and to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the great being endowed with great compassion, it gives a dhāraṇī invoking the powers of intelligence, radiance, and the retention of what one has heard. It…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī for Learning a Thousand Ślokas is a brief ritual text devoted to the noble bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (Toh 1045)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Learning a Thousand Ślokas is a brief ritual text devoted to the noble bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, intended to strengthen memory and the capacity for learning. After paying homage to the Three Jewels and to Avalokiteśvara, it gives a short Sanskrit incantation and then a simple rite. The practitioner makes a maṇḍala before an image of the bodhisattva, presents whatever offerings…

item.title: Dhāraṇī for Mastering a Thousand Ślokas (Toh 1046)
item.description: This brief work, known in English as the Dhāraṇī for Mastering a Thousand Ślokas, is a short incantation text devoted to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the great being endowed with great compassion. After paying homage to the Three Jewels, the Buddha, and Avalokiteśvara, it presents a compact mantra along with simple ritual instructions. Reciting the mantra seven times over water and washing…

item.title: Avalokiteśvara Dhāraṇī for the Sweet Flag Root Rite (Toh 1047)
item.description: This short work, known in English as The Dhāraṇī for Mastering Three Thousand Ślokas, is a brief ritual and incantatory text, a dhāraṇī, dedicated to the noble bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the great being endowed with great compassion. After homages to the Three Jewels and to Avalokiteśvara, it gives a short mantra and instructs the practitioner to make a maṇḍala before the bodhisattva, recite the…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī of Non-forgetting (Toh 1048)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī of Non-forgetting is a very brief incantation text, known in Tibetan by a title meaning "the dhāraṇī for not forgetting," and preserved in the Kangyur as Toh 1048, where it belongs among the dhāraṇī texts. It opens with homage to the Three Jewels and to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, then presents a short Sanskrit mantra invoking memory, mind, and radiant knowledge. The text gives a…

item.title: Homage to the Three Jewels (Toh 1049)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Making Prostrations is a very brief ritual text that opens with homage to the Three Jewels and then teaches a short mantra to be recited before a representation of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, with a full-length prostration made at each recitation. It promises that three such prostrations bring merit equal to hearing, contemplating, and meditating on the entire…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called "Invulnerable to Epidemics and Creatures" (Toh 1050)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called "Invulnerable to Epidemics and Creatures," known in Tibetan as Phakpa Rim Dang Sokchak Kyi Mi Tsukpa Zhejawé Zung, is a very brief protective incantation preserved in Tibetan translation. After a homage to the Three Jewels, it presents a single mantra that invokes Parṇaśabarī, a goddess associated with healing and protection from disease. It then gives a simple ritual…

item.title: The Pacifier of Poison (Toh 1051)
item.description: The Pacifier of Poison, known in Tibetan as Dug zhi bar byed pa, is a very short dhāraṇī, a protective incantation meant to be recited to neutralize poisons of every kind. It opens with homage to Vasudhārā, here called the goddess of nectar medicine, and then gives a brief mantra followed by a declaration of truth: by the truth and splendor of the buddhas, the poisons of nāgas and snakes…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī Called "Luster That Cannot Be Stolen Away" (Toh 1052)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī Called "Luster That Cannot Be Stolen Away," known in Tibetan as Mdangs phyir mi 'phrog pa, is a very brief protective incantation whose Sanskrit title is not securely attested. It opens with homage to Vaiḍūryaprabha, the buddha whose name means "Beryl Light," and then gives a short mantra in Sanskrit invoking protection. A simple ritual instruction follows: a paste of musk, sweet…

item.title: The Noble Terrifying All Māras (Toh 1053)
item.description: The Noble Text Called Terrifying All Māras, known in Tibetan as Phakpa Dü Tamché Trakpar Jepa, is a very brief dhāraṇī that the colophon also names The Dhāraṇī That Terrifies the Māras. After an opening homage to the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, it presents a single Sanskrit mantra invoking the jewel-like radiance of all the tathāgatas and the essence of the realm of phenomena. It then states the…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī-Mantra Called Healing Wounds (Toh 1054)
item.description: Healing Wounds, known in Tibetan as Rma ’byor bar byed pa zhes bya ba’i gzungs sngags, is a very brief dhāraṇī-mantra, a short incantation recited for a specific practical benefit; no Sanskrit title is given in the source. After an opening homage to the noble Mañjuśrī, it presents a single mantra and explains that reciting it three times and smearing spittle on the wound will heal many kinds of…

item.title: Mantra Rite for Learning and Memory (Toh 1034)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for a Melodious Voice is a very short ritual text, a dhāraṇī, which pairs a brief Sanskrit mantra invoking the goddess as Bhagavatī with simple instructions for its use. After an opening homage to the Three Jewels, it directs the practitioner to recite the mantra seven times over a palmful of water each morning for seven days, in the presence of the noble Avalokiteśvara, and then to…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī for Release from Bondage (Toh 1035)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Release from Bondage is a very brief incantation text that opens with homage to the noble Avalokiteśvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, and then presents a single short mantra. The mantra invokes Tārā, the female saviour closely associated with Avalokiteśvara, and calls upon her as the one who frees from bonds. The text then promises that reciting this mantra of the noble one…

item.title: The Vidyā-Mantra of Attaining the Supreme (Toh 1036)
item.description: The Vidyā-Mantra of Attaining the Supreme, known in Sanskrit as the Agravidyāmantra, is a brief ritual text centered on a single incantation addressed to the goddess Śaṅkhinī. After paying homage to her, it lists the mantra's benefits: completing the preliminary approach practice, increasing splendor, wealth, power, retinue, and lifespan, and pacifying enemies and obstructing forces. It instructs…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī Called Increasing Wisdom (Toh 1037)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī Called Generating Wisdom, known in Sanskrit as the Prajñāvardhanī nāma Dhāraṇī and carried in Tibetan under a title of the same meaning, is a brief ritual text centered on a spell for increasing wisdom and mental capacity. It opens on the slopes of Mount Meru, where the bodhisattva Matimān, addressed here as the Blessed One, is teaching the Dharma to the gods who dwell on the…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī Called Increasing Wisdom (Toh 1038)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī Called Increasing Wisdom, known in Sanskrit as the Prajñāvardhanī Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Sherab Kyepa, is a very short incantation text addressed to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. After paying homage to the Three Jewels and to Avalokiteśvara, it gives a brief mantra and a simple accompanying rite: one recites the mantra three times over a palmful of water and drinks it, and after…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī Called "Increasing Wisdom" (Toh 1039)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī Called "Increasing Wisdom," known in Sanskrit as the Prajñāvardhanī nāma dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Sherab Kyepa Zhejawai Zung, is a brief incantatory text that pays homage to the Three Jewels and to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the great compassionate one. It then gives a short mantra invoking the growth of wisdom, intelligence, and understanding. The text closes with a simple rite…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī for Retaining What Is Heard (Toh 1040)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Retaining What Is Heard is a very brief incantation text in which the speaker pays homage to the Three Jewels and to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the great being associated with compassion. It then gives a short mantra invoking memory and intelligence. Its title is known here in English from its closing line, and its Sanskrit and Tibetan names are not preserved in the opening…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī That Increases Wisdom (Toh 1041)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Retaining What Has Been Heard is a brief incantatory text belonging to the dhāraṇī genre, short formulas of power recited for specific spiritual and practical benefits. After paying homage to the Three Jewels and to the Buddha Śākyamuni, it gives a single Sanskrit spell invoking wisdom, the lamp of insight, and the dispelling of darkness, followed by a concise ritual instruction…

item.title: Dhāraṇī of Avalokiteśvara for Retention of What Is Heard and Remembered (Toh 1042)
item.description: The Learning of a Hundred Ślokas is a brief dhāraṇī text, a short ritual incantation for strengthening memory and learning. After paying homage to the Three Jewels and to the noble bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the great being endowed with great compassion, it gives a single dhāraṇī that invokes illumination, purification, the fulfillment of beings' wishes, and the retention of what is heard and…

item.title: Learning a Hundred Verses (Toh 1043)
item.description: Learning a Hundred Ślokas is a very brief text that opens with homage to the Three Jewels and to the noble bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the great being endowed with great compassion. It presents a short mantra and a simple ritual instruction: while washing the face, one recites the mantra three or seven times over a handful of water and then drinks it. This practice is said to let a person learn a…

item.title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra called The Samādhi of Heroic Progress (Toh 132)
item.description: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra called The Samādhi of Heroic Progress, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Śūraṅgamasamādhi Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Pawar Drowé Tingngedzin, is a Mahāyāna sūtra devoted to a powerful meditative absorption, the "heroic progress" samādhi, through which bodhisattvas advance fearlessly along the path to awakening. The discourse opens on Vulture Peak near…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī Thoroughly Pacifying All Misdeeds (Toh 1023)
item.description: Thoroughly Pacifying All Misdeeds is a very brief dhāraṇī text whose Sanskrit and Tibetan titles are not given in the opening lines. After homage to the Three Jewels and to the Buddha as Tathāgata, arhat, and perfectly complete Buddha, it consists almost entirely of a single incantation. The incantation calls upon Mañjuśrī in his youthful form, urging him to come quickly, to free the reciter from…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī That Pacifies Anger (Toh 1025)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī That Pacifies Anger, known in Tibetan as Khro ba zhi bar byed pa'i gzungs, is a very brief ritual text centered on a single mantra invoking the Blessed One to subdue, stupefy, and calm all wrath. After an opening homage to the Three Jewels, it gives the mantra and a simple instruction: sitting facing east, one recites it, wipes one's face seven times with one's own hand, and then…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī That Pacifies Anger (Toh 1026)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī That Pacifies Anger, known in Tibetan as Pakpa Tröpa Shiwar Jepé Zung, is a very short incantation text whose Sanskrit title is not securely attested but would correspond to a noble dhāraṇī for the pacification of anger. After a brief homage to Mahāśrī, the Great Glorious One, it gives a single mantra and explains its use: when recited in the presence of someone who is angry…

item.title: Toh 1027 (Toh 1027)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī of Powerful Speech is a brief ritual incantation that opens with homage to the Three Jewels and a short mantra invoking the Blessed One as the uṣṇīṣa, the crown protuberance of a buddha. Its Sanskrit and Tibetan titles cannot be determined with confidence from the surviving title lines. The text promises that its formula works even without prior practice. It then sets out a series of…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī for Protecting Oneself (Toh 1028)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Protecting Oneself is a very brief protective incantation from the Buddhist tradition. After a homage to the Three Jewels, it gives a short mantra and a simple ritual instruction. The practitioner faces the sun, recites the mantra seven times over water, and then scatters the water in the ten directions to secure personal protection. The source lines do not clearly preserve its…

item.title: Homage to the King of Lunar Days, Constellations, and Moments (Toh 1029)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Accomplishing All Aims is a very short incantation text, known in Tibetan under a title that expresses the same idea of bringing every purpose to fulfillment. After paying homage to the Three Jewels, it honors a buddha called the King of Lunar Days, Constellations, and Moments, a name that evokes the astrological reckoning of auspicious times. It then gives a brief Sanskrit…

item.title: Toh 1030 (Toh 1030)
item.description: This short work, catalogued without a clearly preserved title in its opening lines, is a dhāraṇī, a sacred incantation in Sanskrit-based syllables, introduced by homage to the Three Jewels, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. After the spell itself, which invokes a series of goddess-like names and leaves blanks where the practitioner inserts the name of the person concerned, the text sets out…

item.title: Dhāraṇī for Obtaining Garments (Toh 1031)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Obtaining a Hundred Garments is a very brief ritual text from the Kangyur's collection of dhāraṇīs. It opens with homage to the Three Jewels and to the fierce Vajrapāṇi, called here the great general of the yakṣas. It then gives a short mantra-like incantation and explains how to use it: one recites it a thousand times over a single set of garments and then gives the garments to a…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī That Causes Displeasure (Toh 1032)
item.description: This brief work, known in English as The Dhāraṇī That Causes Displeasure, is listed as Toh 1032 in the Kangyur, where it belongs to the class of dhāraṇī texts, the collection of incantations and spells preserved within the canon. Its Sanskrit and Tibetan titles are not stated in the opening lines, and the text itself is extremely short. After a homage to the Three Jewels, it gives a single mantra…

item.title: The Noble One Called "Pleasing" (Toh 1033)
item.description: The Noble One Called "Pleasing," known in Tibetan as Phakpa Yidu Ongwa Zhejawa and concluding under the name The Pleasing Dhāraṇī, is a very brief ritual text built around a short mantra addressed to the uṣṇīṣa, the crown protuberance of a buddha. After an opening homage to the buddhas, it gives the mantra and says it works through recitation alone, without any prior practice. It then describes…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called "Thoroughly Pacifying All Illnesses" (Toh 1014)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called "Thoroughly Pacifying All Illnesses," known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Sarvaroga­praśamani Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Pakpa Né Tamché Rabtu Shiwar Jepa Shejawé Sung, is a brief dhāraṇī text that offers a protective incantation for healing a wide range of bodily ailments. Set in Prince Jeta's Grove at Śrāvastī, it opens with the Buddha urging the assembled monks to take…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī That Thoroughly Pacifies Illness (Toh 1015)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī That Thoroughly Pacifies Illness, known in Tibetan as Phakpa Né Rabtu Zhiwar Jepé Zung and probably corresponding to a Sanskrit title along the lines of Ārya Roga Praśamanī Dhāraṇī, is a very brief incantation text devoted to healing. After paying homage to the Three Jewels and to the Buddha under the name Vajra Guru King, it gives a short mantra that invokes the vajra and calls…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called "Completely Pacifying Fever" (Toh 1016)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called "Completely Pacifying Fever," known in Sanskrit as the Āryajvarapraśamanināmadhāraṇī and in Tibetan as 'Phags pa rims nad rab tu zhi bar byed pa zhes bya ba'i gzungs, is a short protective scripture meant to relieve those afflicted by fever. It opens at the great charnel ground of Śītavana near Rājagṛha, where a monk asks the Buddha to protect beings tormented by fever…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī for Pacifying Epidemic Disease (Toh 1017)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Pacifying Epidemic Disease is a very brief protective incantation preserved in Tibetan translation, and its Sanskrit and Tibetan titles are known chiefly from its closing line, which names it after its purpose of calming epidemic illness. After paying homage to the Three Jewels and to the Buddha Amitābha, the text gives a short mantra that names the person to be protected and…

item.title: The Noble Sūtra That Thoroughly Pacifies Eye Disease (Toh 1018)
item.description: The Noble Sūtra That Thoroughly Pacifies Eye Disease, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Akṣirogapraśamanisūtra and in Tibetan as Phags pa mig nad rab tu zhi bar byed pa'i mdo, is a brief scripture concerned with healing afflictions of the eyes. Set on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, it opens with the great yakṣa general known as the Black One approaching the Buddha and asking how eye diseases…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī That Pacifies the Disease of Smallpox (Toh 1019)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī That Pacifies the Disease of Smallpox is a very brief incantatory text whose title is known here in English. Its Sanskrit and Tibetan titles cannot be determined with confidence from the source at hand. After a simple homage to the Three Jewels, it consists almost entirely of a single dhāraṇī, a Sanskrit spell addressed to the Blessed Mañjuśrī in his youthful form. The spell invokes…

item.title: The Noble Sūtra That Thoroughly Pacifies Hemorrhoids (Toh 1020)
item.description: The Noble Sūtra That Thoroughly Pacifies Hemorrhoids, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Arśapraśamanī and in Tibetan as Phakpa Zhangdrum Raptu Zhiwar Jepé Do, is a short Mahāyāna scripture that offers a healing incantation for relief from this painful affliction. The text opens at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, where the Buddha is seated before a great assembly of monks on the full-moon observance…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī for Clearing Away the Illness of Indigestion (Toh 1021)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Clearing Away the Illness of Indigestion is a very brief healing incantation, and its Sanskrit and Tibetan titles are not given in the material available here. After paying homage to the Three Jewels and to the Tathāgata called King of the Radiance of Fire, it presents a short mantra and a simple accompanying rite: one recites the mantra over one's hand and then rubs the belly…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī Completely Pacifying All Hostility (Toh 1022)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called "Completely Pacifying All Hostility" is a very brief incantation text, known in Tibetan as a gzungs, or dhāraṇī. It opens with homage to the Three Jewels and to the Buddha Samantadarśin, the "All-Seeing," and then gives a short mantra. Its instruction is that anyone who recites the mantra seven times while supplicating the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī will find that all people…

item.title: The Dharma Text of the Buddha's Treasury (Toh 123)
item.description: The Dharma Text of the Buddha's Treasury, known in Tibetan as Sangs rgyas kyi mdzod kyi chos kyi yi ge, is a Mahāyāna sūtra that also bears the alternative title The Instruction Given on All Phenomena. Set on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha before a great assembly of monks and countless bodhisattvas, it opens with Śāriputra rising from meditation to question the Buddha about his teaching that…

item.title: The Noble Sūtra of Mahālakṣmī (Toh 1005)
item.description: The Noble Sūtra of Mahālakṣmī, known in Sanskrit as the Āryamahālakṣmīsūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Pal Chenmö Do, is a brief scripture centered on the goddess of fortune and prosperity, Mahālakṣmī. Set in the pure land of Sukhāvatī, it opens as the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara approaches the Blessed One. The Buddha then turns his attention toward Mahālakṣmī and declares that anyone who knows her…

item.title: The Twelve Names of the Goddess Śrī (Toh 1006)
item.description: The Twelve Names of the Goddess Śrī, known in Tibetan as Pal gyi Lhamo'i Tsen Chunyipa, is a short scripture devoted to Śrī, or Lakṣmī, the great goddess of fortune and prosperity. It opens in the realm of Sukhāvatī, where the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the great goddess Śrī, herself honored here as a bodhisattva and great being, come before the Blessed One. The Buddha then turns to…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called Vasudhārā (Toh 1007)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called Vasudhārā, known in Sanskrit as Āryavasudhārānāmadhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Phakpa Nor gyi Gyün zhejawé Zung, is a short scripture centered on a dhāraṇī, a sacred incantation associated with Vasudhārā, the goddess whose name means "stream of wealth." The text opens at Kauśāmbī, where the Buddha is staying in the Kaṇṭaka forest with a great assembly of monks and…

item.title: The Noble Vidyā-Mantra Called Purifying the Eye (Toh 1008)
item.description: The Noble Vidyā-Mantra Called Purifying the Eye, known in Sanskrit as Āryacakṣurviśodhanī nāma vidyāmantra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Mik Nampar Jongwa Zhejawé Rikngak, is a short scripture centered on a vidyāmantra, a spell of awareness, whose title points to the purification and healing of the eyes. It opens in the classic sutra manner, with the Blessed One staying among the Śākyas, and introduces…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called "Completely Purifying All Karmic Obscurations" (Toh 1009)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called Completely Purifying All Karmic Obscurations, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhanī Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Phakpa Le Kyi Dripa Tamche Nampar Jongwa Shyejawé Zung, is a brief incantation text centered on a single dhāraṇī-mantra. Opening with homage to the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, it presents the mantra and then explains its rite and benefits. Constant…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī-Mantra That Dispels All Obstacles (Toh 1010)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī-Mantra That Dispels All Obstacles, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Sarvāntarasaṃgrāsa Dhāraṇī Mantra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Bardu Chöpa Tamché Selwé Zung Ngak, is a short dhāraṇī text in which the Blessed One addresses the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi about the protective power of a sacred incantation. The Buddha explains that anyone who upholds, carries, and recites this dhāraṇī-mantra…
